My work asks how digital media reshape the relationship between political elites and
citizens. Three strands run through it: how elites *target* and communicate, what
citizens are *able to tell* about the content that reaches them, and how elite media
strategy translates into public standing. A fourth, newer strand looks at what happens
in the discussions themselves.

## Political microtargeting

::: {.theme}
::: {.theme-kicker}
Elite strategy
:::

Online political advertising lets parties address different voter groups with different
messages, largely out of public view. My dissertation, *The Nature and Consequences of
Online Political Microtargeting*, asks what parties actually do with that capacity and
what follows from it.

Rather than treating targeting as a black box, I use the targeting criteria parties
themselves select as data. This yields a **targeting ideology** measure: an inference
about how political elites perceive and sort the electorate, drawn from their own
advertising choices. Across multi-party systems, the pattern that emerges is less
sophisticated persuasion of swing voters than reinforcement of existing constituencies —
parties largely preach to their own choirs.

The work is comparative as well as Danish: with colleagues I have mapped microtargeting
usage worldwide, documenting how unevenly the practice is distributed across countries
and party families.
:::

## AI-generated content and misinformation

::: {.theme}
::: {.theme-kicker}
Citizen responses
:::

Generative AI has made synthetic images cheap and abundant. A basic democratic question
follows: can people tell? In large-scale studies with colleagues from Copenhagen, Aarhus,
and SDU, we find that most people **cannot** reliably distinguish AI-generated images from
photographs — detection accuracy sits far closer to chance than most people assume of
themselves.

This line of work connects to a broader interest in the role of digital platforms in the
information environment, which I have also written about for the Danish Ministry of
Digitalisation.
:::

## Elite media strategy and public standing

::: {.theme}
::: {.theme-kicker}
Elites and the public
:::

Politicians invest heavily in visibility. Does it pay? Working with Danish ministers, I
examine how media activity relates to public approval and name recognition — and for
*whom* that effort registers. The answer is not uniform across the electorate, which
raises questions about who the audience for political communication effectively is.
:::

## Online political discussion

::: {.theme}
::: {.theme-kicker}
Work in progress
:::

Comment sections under posts from politicians and news outlets are one of the few places
where elites and citizens meet in public. I am currently working on what these discussions
look like from both sides: how politicians manage and moderate the spaces they open, and
what draws citizens into them.
:::

## Methods

I collect and analyse large social media datasets through platforms' research APIs and
combine several approaches depending on the question:

- **Text-as-data and LLM-based classification** for large corpora of political messages
  and comments
- **Survey research and (field) experiments** for questions about citizen perception and
  effects
- **Descriptive and measurement work** — systematically documenting phenomena that are
  often asserted but rarely measured, and building new indicators where none exist

Nearly all of it happens in R.
